The four cases of the course were chosen from the work of SCORE, a research programme that tested the claims of published social and behavioural research in three different ways, and the exercise that each case teaches repeats on a small scale the design of Multi100, the study of the programme in which other analysts reanalysed the data behind those claims. This page describes the programme and its three studies, the way in which Multi100 chose its claims and organised the work of its analysts, and what the record of the programme holds for each of the four cases. How Multi100 made the results of its analysts comparable, and what its article reports, is the subject of [a page of its own](multi100-article.qmd).

## The programme {#sec-score}

SCORE, short for Systematizing Confidence in Open Research and Evidence, was a programme funded by DARPA, the research agency of the United States Department of Defense, which put claims from published social and behavioural research through three kinds of repetition [@AlipourfardEtAl2021SystematizingConfidenceOpen]. A reproduction repeats the original analysis on the original data, a robustness check applies different but defensible analyses to the same data, and a replication asks the same question of new data. The three studies, which were reported together in *Nature* in 2026, shared one sampling frame, for which "a stratified random sample of 600 articles was identified from a larger pool of approximately 30,000 randomly stratified articles across 62 journals published between 2009 and 2018" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, Methods], and in each article the central claim was traced from the abstract to the statistical result that supports it.

The reproducibility study asked the authors of the 600 papers for their data and code [@MiskeEtAl2026InvestigatingReproducibilitySocial]. The authors of 144 papers (24.0%) made their data available, and the team rebuilt the datasets of 38 others from source data, so that 182 datasets were in hand, of which 143 were assessed. Of these papers, 53.6% were rated as precisely reproducible and 73.5% as at least approximately reproducible, that is, "within 15% of the original effects or within 0.05 of original P values" [@MiskeEtAl2026InvestigatingReproducibilitySocial, p. 126]. Reproducibility was higher in political science and economics than in the other fields, in more recent papers, and in papers from journals that require their authors to share data (p. 126).

The replicability study tested 274 claims of positive results from 164 quantitative papers, published in 54 of the journals, with replications that had a median power of 99.6% to detect the original effect size [@TynerEtAl2026InvestigatingReplicabilitySocial, p. 143]. The replications showed a statistically significant result in the original pattern for 151 of the 274 claims (55.1%), and the median effect size, as a Pearson correlation, fell from 0.25 in the original studies to 0.10 in the replications. Whether a replication succeeds is itself a matter of method, since the thirteen ways of judging success that the study applied gave rates from 28.6% to 74.8% (p. 143).

The robustness study was Multi100 [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness], the subject of the rest of this page.

## Multi100 {#sec-multi100}

Multi100 set out to measure how far published conclusions and results depend on the choices of the analyst who produced them. Its preregistration gives the main aim as "to estimate the degree to which published conclusions and results in social and behavioural sciences are robust to the analytical choices of analysts", and it asks two questions: "Do different analysts arrive at the same conclusions as the analyst of the original study? Do different analysts arrive at the same effect estimates (+/- 0.05 Cohen's d) as the analyst of the original study?" ([osf.io/4ev9t](https://osf.io/4ev9t), p. 2).

The claims came from the first phase of SCORE, in which a single claim had been extracted from the abstract of each article, one that "ideally corresponded to one statistically significant inferential test result" (preregistration, p. 5). The lead team of Multi100 kept the claims that were understandable, contained only one claim, indicated the direction of the effect and had a test in the article that corresponded to them (p. 5), and where it judged an expression of a claim "ambiguous or rhetorical", it replaced the expression with an ellipsis "while preserving the original wording and the meaning of the claim" (p. 5). The ellipses in the claims of the four cases come from this step. The published Methods add that each selected study had to contain "a single inferential statistical test result that corresponded to the claim with our instructions" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, Methods].

Each claim went to at least five analysts, who worked independently with the data of the original study and with the full article in hand, since the lead team "opted for complete transparency of the original article so that no potentially important information is missing for the co-analyst" (preregistration, p. 4). The analysts received the claim but no research question, as the preregistration states: "We will provide the co-analysts with the above described claims to test on the original datasets but we will not give them specific research questions" (p. 5). In all, 457 analysts produced 504 reanalyses of 100 studies [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, p. 136], and Chris Moreh, who leads this course, was one of the analysts.

The work came in two tasks. In the first, the analysts could "conduct and report as many analyses as they wish but they will have to draw a single conclusion from their analysis" (preregistration, p. 7), choosing between evidence for the claim, evidence for the opposite effect, evidence neither way and evidence for the null hypothesis (p. 8). In the second, each analyst produced "only one statistical result corresponding to the claim they studied in Task 1, which will be compared to a statistical result in the original paper", under instructions of the lead team on matters such as "data selection, exclusions" (p. 7). The published Methods explain why both tasks were needed, the first answering the question about conclusions and the second the question about effect estimates, since "asking only one of the tasks would not have been sufficient to fully address both questions" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, Methods], and a panel of peers then judged whether each analysis was appropriate.

The instruction of the second task is where the case study of each case picks up the story, because it settled some of the decisions that the five analysts of the case faced and left others to the analysts. Much of the spread among the five results of a case arguably comes from the decisions that the instruction left open.

## The four cases in the record {#sec-cases}

The record of the programme differs from case to case. The table gives, for each of the four claims, the outcome of the reproduction and of the replication, and the conclusions that the five Multi100 analysts reached in the first task.

| Case | Original study | Reproduction | Robustness | Replication |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| [Housing audit](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing/) | a field experiment in the *American Journal of Political Science* [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect] | never attempted, although the data and code are public | three of the five analysts found evidence for the claim, two evidence neither way | a preregistered audit of 3,050 housing authorities found no significant gap |
| [Immigration and trust](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-immigration/) | an analysis of the European Social Survey in *World Politics* [@McLaren2012CulturalDivideEurope] | two reproductions from the survey files, close to the published coefficient but on fewer respondents | all five found evidence for the claim | two replications on later rounds of the survey met the criterion of SCORE |
| [Cohabitation](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-cohabitation/) | an analysis of union histories in *Demography* [@KuoRaley2016DivergingPatternsUnion] | none recorded | two found evidence for the claim, one evidence neither way and two the opposite | the replication tested another coefficient of the paper and did not replicate it |
| [EU frames](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-eu/) | an analysis of Eurobarometer surveys in the *European Sociological Review* [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic] | two attempts from the original materials, neither successful | all five found evidence for the claim | judged not successful on later Eurobarometer waves |

Read across the rows, the three kinds of repetition do not move together. The EU-frames claim, which every analyst upheld in the first task, could be neither reproduced from its original materials nor replicated on later waves of its survey, while the immigration-and-trust claim, upheld just as consistently, replicated on later rounds of the European Social Survey. Four cases are far too few for a conclusion about the literature, but they show, case by case, why the course keeps the three questions apart, and each case site tells the story of its own row in its case study.

## The exercise of the course {#sec-course}

The exercise of the course repeats the design of Multi100 with the class in the place of its analysts. Each participant receives the claim and the data of a case, writes an estimand statement, which names the quantity that an analysis of the claim should estimate, and reproduces the result that Multi100 recorded for one of the five analysts of the case, from the data behind it. In the formats that take the exercise further, the participant then works through the decisions that lie between the data and a result, declares one specification in a short preregistration before running it, and sends the result to a class chart, on which it sits beside the results of the rest of the class, those of the five analysts and the curve of the claim, so that each participant becomes a sixth analyst of the claim. Each case closes on its replication, which asks what new data add to what the reanalyses showed. The [page on the Multi100 article](multi100-article.qmd) takes up the comparison of results on a common scale, on which the meta-analysis modules of the case sites build.
